paragraphs: Graph neural networks can perform differently depending on the properties of the graphs they receive. This paper investigates those differences by analyzing information collected from existing benchmarks. Instead of beginning with a manually chosen explanation of model behavior, it looks for relationships between dataset properties and measured GNN performance across diverse datasets.

The authors use multivariate sparse regression to identify a small set of influential properties while considering several properties together. They then examine one identified factor in detail: the degree distribution, which describes how the number of connections varies across nodes. This turns a pattern found in benchmark metadata into a specific question that theoretical analysis and controlled experiments can investigate.

Their analysis links more balanced degree distributions to node representations that are easier to separate with a linear classifier, supporting better GNN performance. Experiments on synthetic graphs with varying degree distributions agree with the theoretical findings. Together, these results support metadata analysis as a useful way to identify consequential graph properties and direct deeper investigations of GNN behavior.
neurips-2023-a-metadata-driven-approach-.tldr: Benchmark metadata helps identify graph properties that affect GNN performance, with degree distribution validated through theory and controlled experiments.

paragraphs: Domain incremental learning asks a model to adapt to a sequence of domains while retaining only a small sample of data from earlier ones. Many methods address this setting, but their relationships can be difficult to understand. This paper introduces Unified Domain Incremental Learning, or UDIL, to place several existing approaches within a shared theoretical framework.

The central connection is a bound on generalization error: a theoretical expression controlling how well learning can transfer beyond the observed data. Existing methods correspond to different fixed choices of coefficients in that bound. UDIL allows those coefficients to adapt during training. Within this formulation, the authors show that adaptive choices achieve the tightest bound and yield a tighter guarantee than the methods they unify.

The framework therefore provides both an explanation of existing approaches and a way to improve their coefficient choices. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than state-of-the-art domain incremental learning methods. These empirical gains complement the theoretical result: the bound establishes an advantage in the analysis, while the experiments demonstrate improved performance on the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2023-a-unified-approach-to-domai.tldr: UDIL unifies memory-based domain incremental learning methods and adaptively chooses coefficients to tighten its generalization bound.

paragraphs: Text-driven motion generation needs to capture more than an action name. Small details in a description can distinguish otherwise similar movements, yet compact sentence representations may give those details too little influence. This paper introduces hierarchical semantic graphs to make the different parts of a motion description explicit and available for finer control.

The graphs organize descriptions into three levels: the overall motion, individual actions, and their specifics. The authors mirror that organization in the motion diffusion process, dividing generation into corresponding semantic levels. This connects the structure of the description to the structure of generation, allowing broad movement information and local action details to guide synthesis at appropriate levels.

Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT report superior performance and support the effectiveness of this structured approach. The method also allows continuous refinement of generated movement by changing graph edge weights. Those weights provide an adjustable way to influence the relationships represented in the description, making the graph useful both for understanding the requested motion and for controlling its generation.
neurips-2023-act-as-you-wish-fine-graine.tldr: Hierarchical semantic graphs guide motion diffusion at three levels and enable continuous control through adjustable graph weights.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from fMRI data requires recovering its meaning as well as its appearance. Existing methods can produce high-quality images while becoming uncertain about what they depict when test examples differ semantically from training examples. This paper develops GESS to address that gap explicitly during image reconstruction.

GESS combines two sources of guidance. A pretrained CLIP model maps training examples into compact features that expand the coverage of their semantic information, helping with examples near known concepts within the training super-classes. For examples farther from those concepts, the method uses structural information motivated by the robust low-level representations available in fMRI data. These two sources address different degrees of semantic distance.

The method estimates semantic uncertainty using probability density estimation and adaptively combines semantic and structural guidance within a diffusion process. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art reconstruction methods. The authors also propose a data-splitting strategy for evaluating generalized reconstruction, making the semantic gap an explicit part of assessment rather than judging only the quality of images from familiar concepts.
neurips-2023-alleviating-the-semantic-ga.tldr: GESS adaptively combines expanded semantic features and structural guidance to improve fMRI-to-image reconstruction across semantic gaps.

paragraphs: Image and text models need a shared representation to compare information across the two modalities. Building that representation often involves training encoders on paired images and descriptions. ASIF shows that existing single-domain encoders can be connected without additional training, using a much smaller collection of image-text pairs.

The paired dataset serves as a reference for constructing the common space. Each dimension represents how similar an input is to a particular dataset entry. Because the entries link images with text, these similarity representations provide a connection between the otherwise separate encoders. They also make individual dimensions interpretable: a coordinate refers to a specific reference example rather than an unexplained learned feature.

Experiments on standard zero-shot visual benchmarks demonstrate the transfer abilities associated with image-text models. The authors also report that updating the reference samples allows a new version to be deployed within seconds. The contribution is a simple, strong baseline showing how much multimodal capability can come from existing encoders and coupled data, prompting closer examination of data efficiency and retrieval.
neurips-2023-asif-coupled-data-turns-uni.tldr: ASIF connects existing image and text encoders through paired reference data, creating an interpretable shared space without additional training.

paragraphs: As foundation-model training datasets grow, determining whether a particular example was included becomes difficult. This paper proposes Data Portraits: accompanying artifacts that record information about training data and support later inspection. The goal is to make questions about data exposure answerable through dataset documentation that can be queried.

The authors first describe desirable properties of these artifacts and discuss how existing solutions could improve transparency. They then implement an approach based on data sketching, which creates a compact representation designed for fast queries. They use it to document The Pile, a language-modeling corpus, and The Stack, a dataset for code modeling.

The resulting tool supports investigations of test-set leakage and model plagiarism by helping inspect whether relevant material appears in the documented data. Its storage overhead is reported as only 3% of dataset size, making the added record comparatively lightweight. The authors release a live interface and encourage dataset and model creators to distribute Data Portraits alongside their existing documentation, giving downstream users a practical way to examine training-data provenance.
neurips-2023-data-portraits-recording-fo.tldr: Data Portraits provide compact, searchable training-data records that support transparency and investigations of leakage and plagiarism.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often alternates between estimating values and extracting a policy from those estimates. Errors can propagate as the two stages repeatedly influence each other. DROP separates these tasks in time: value estimation happens during training, while policy extraction happens during testing, creating a non-iterative relationship between the two levels.

This separation requires deciding what information to pass forward and how to use it conservatively. Drawing on model-based optimization, DROP splits the offline data into subsets and learns a score model. It also learns a representation of behavior and introduces conservative regularization to guide how the score model is exploited when selecting a policy.

Performing policy optimization during testing allows deployment adaptation, with inference adapting across states. This gives the separation a practical purpose beyond avoiding repeated error propagation: policy extraction can respond at deployment time. Experiments across various tasks show performance comparable to or better than prior methods. The results support this alternative organization of offline policy optimization, combining learned scores with constraints on their use.
neurips-2023-design-from-policies-conser.tldr: DROP separates offline value learning from conservative policy optimization at test time, enabling adaptation during deployment.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, an agent may need to explore extensively before discovering useful behavior. ELDEN addresses environments whose states can be divided into entities with chained dependencies: an action changes one entity, which can then affect another. It defines interesting situations through uncertainty about whether those influences exist.

The method learns a dynamics model and uses its partial derivatives to estimate local dependencies between entities. These derivatives capture how predicted changes relate to different parts of the state. Uncertainty in the predicted dependency structure becomes an intrinsic reward, encouraging the agent to discover new interactions. The focus is on uncertainty about the presence of influence, rather than only uncertainty about the exact outcome of an interaction.

Evaluations cover four domains with complex dependencies, ranging from two-dimensional grid worlds to three-dimensional robotic tasks. In all four, ELDEN identifies local dependencies and learns successful policies, significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art exploration methods. These results support interaction discovery as an effective exploration signal for the factored, dependency-rich environments studied.
neurips-2023-elden-exploration-via-local.tldr: ELDEN rewards uncertainty about interactions between entities to guide exploration in environments with complex dependencies.

paragraphs: Few-shot class-incremental learning requires adding new categories from very few labeled examples while preserving knowledge of earlier categories. This paper identifies a recurring problem: models tend to assign examples from new classes to the established base classes. Strong separation among the base classes can therefore coexist with poor recognition of newly introduced ones.

The authors observe that a feature extractor trained only on base classes can still represent semantic similarities between those classes and unseen categories. TEEN uses this information to adjust new-class prototypes, where a prototype is the mean feature representation of a class. It combines each new prototype with weighted base-class prototypes, using existing semantic relationships to improve the distinction of new categories without additional training.

This approach makes the learned base-class structure a resource for calibrating new representations. The paper reports strong performance on standard class-incremental benchmarks and consistent improvements over baseline methods in the broader few-shot learning setting. The findings suggest that correcting the representation of new classes can be useful even when the feature extractor already contains relevant semantic information.
neurips-2023-few-shot-class-incremental-.tldr: TEEN improves few-shot recognition by calibrating new-class prototypes with weighted base-class prototypes without additional training.

paragraphs: Graph augmentation creates additional training examples to help graph classifiers generalize and remain robust. A graph contains both connections and signals associated with its nodes, but existing augmentation approaches often handle these separately. This paper develops a way to mix graphs while accounting for the interaction between their structure and signals.

FGWMixup formulates node matching between source graphs as an optimal transport problem. Its matching strategy considers both kinds of information, then seeks a midpoint between the graphs in the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein metric space. This gives the mixing operation a joint notion of similarity, so the resulting augmentation reflects how node information and graph connections fit together.

To improve scalability, the authors introduce a relaxed solver whose stated convergence rate improves from O(t^-1) to O(t^-2). Experiments on five datasets evaluate the augmentation with both message-passing neural networks and Graphormer backbones. The results show improved generalizability and robustness across these tested architectures, supporting joint treatment of graph structure and signals as a useful design choice for graph-level classification.
neurips-2023-fused-gromov-wasserstein-gr.tldr: FGWMixup augments graph data by jointly matching and mixing graph structure and node signals through optimal transport.

paragraphs: Curiosity-driven exploration can produce both exploratory trajectories and a learned model of an environment's dynamics. This paper asks how to turn those products into goal-directed behavior without collecting any additional interactions. The task is to reach specified goals using information gathered during exploration that was not organized around those goals.

The authors find that conventional approaches for learning goal-conditioned values and policies struggle in this offline setting. By examining the geometry of optimal goal-conditioned value functions, they connect the problem to particular artifacts in learned value estimates. Such artifacts matter because planning and action selection depend on the shape of those estimates, not merely on having a dynamics model.

Their method combines model-based planning over learned value landscapes with graph-based aggregation of values. The combination can correct both local and global estimation artifacts, addressing problems at different scales. Across diverse simulated environments, it significantly improves zero-shot goal-reaching performance. The result shows a way to make curiosity-generated data more useful for later goals while preserving the requirement of no further environment interaction.
neurips-2023-goal-conditioned-offline-pl.tldr: Combining model-based planning with graph-based value aggregation improves offline goal reaching from curiosity-driven exploration.

paragraphs: Jigsaw tackles the problem of reassembling a physically broken three-dimensional object from multiple pieces. The task requires identifying which surfaces came from fractures, finding compatible locations across pieces, and placing every piece consistently. The framework uses both overall geometry and local surface detail to connect these decisions.

Its pipeline has four components. An attention-based feature extractor describes points on the pieces. Surface segmentation distinguishes broken surfaces from original exterior surfaces, and a matching stage finds corresponding points across fracture surfaces. A robust global alignment stage then recovers the positions and orientations of the pieces. Segmentation and matching are learned jointly, while feature matches are integrated with rigidity constraints that keep each piece geometrically consistent.

On the Breaking Bad dataset, Jigsaw outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report good generalization across fracture patterns, objects, and unseen instances. These findings support combining surface recognition, correspondence learning, and global alignment in one framework for multi-piece assembly. The paper presents the method as, to the authors' knowledge, the first learning-based approach specifically designed for this setting.
neurips-2023-jigsaw-learning-to-assemble.tldr: Jigsaw learns to identify and match fracture surfaces, then globally aligns multiple broken pieces to reconstruct 3D objects.

paragraphs: Vision models benefit from both local details and the broader context of an image. This paper focuses on how those two kinds of information influence one another. It introduces Fully Adaptive Self-Attention, or FASA, to extract local and global representations and let each adapt in response to the other.

FASA uses self-modulated convolutions for local features and self-attention over a downsampled representation for global features. A bidirectional adaptation step connects the two. The authors also introduce a finer-grained downsampling strategy to improve the global information captured by attention. Together, these components aim to retain detailed contextual reasoning while keeping computation suitable for lightweight models.

The resulting Fully Adaptive Transformer family is evaluated on multiple vision tasks. One model achieves 77.6% ImageNet-1K accuracy with 4.5 million parameters and 0.7 billion FLOPs, outperforming advanced convolutional and transformer models with similar resource costs in the reported comparisons. The authors also report faster execution on modern GPUs. These results support explicit local-global interaction as a useful component of efficient vision backbones.
neurips-2023-lightweight-vision-transfor.tldr: FASA enables two-way interaction between local and global image features to build accurate, lightweight vision transformers.

paragraphs: Updating only a small fraction of a pretrained model's parameters does not necessarily make fine-tuning memory-efficient. Gradient computation can still require storing most intermediate activations. This paper addresses that remaining memory cost by making a pretrained model reversible, allowing intermediate activations to be reconstructed instead of kept throughout training.

Converting an existing model is difficult because reversible architectures differ from commonly released pretrained models. The authors first investigate successful parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods and identify preservation of the pretrained starting point at initialization as essential. Their memory-efficient fine-tuning method, MEFT, inserts adapters that preserve that starting point while making the model reversible, without requiring additional pretraining.

MEFT is evaluated on GLUE and five question-answering tasks using BERT, RoBERTa, BART, and OPT backbones. The paper reports activation-memory reductions of up to 84% relative to full fine-tuning, with very few trainable parameters. It matches full fine-tuning's GLUE score and achieves comparable question-answering scores. A similar finding on image classification suggests that the demonstrated benefit extends beyond the evaluated language tasks.
neurips-2023-make-pre-trained-model-reve.tldr: MEFT adds adapters that preserve a pretrained model's starting point while enabling reversible computation and substantially lower activation memory.

paragraphs: Average precision evaluates the ordering of predictions and is useful when positive and negative examples are heavily imbalanced. This paper argues that adversarial robustness measured through classification accuracy can miss important ranking failures. A small perturbation to one example may substantially change average precision while barely affecting overall prediction accuracy.

The proposed objective combines a surrogate loss for average precision with a regularization term for adversarial ranking robustness. That term encourages the ordering of clean examples to remain consistent with the ordering after perturbation. The authors also develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm for this objective, making ranking consistency a direct part of training.

Empirical comparisons against leading adversarial training methods and robust average-precision approaches support the method's effectiveness. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, the paper reports more than 4% higher robust average precision under PGD attacks and 7% higher clean-data average precision than TRADES. These results show improvements in both clean and attacked rankings in the evaluated setting, supporting robustness objectives that directly reflect the ranking metric of interest.
neurips-2023-maximization-of-average-pre.tldr: A ranking-consistency regularizer improves average precision on both clean and adversarially perturbed data in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training a neural network requires memory for optimizer states as well as model parameters. These states can consume enough space to limit the model size that fits within a memory budget. This paper reduces their representation to four bits, extending the compression beyond the eight-bit states described as the previous lowest achievable precision.

The method follows an empirical analysis of first- and second-moment statistics. The authors find complicated outlier patterns that existing block-wise quantization does not approximate accurately. They use smaller blocks and incorporate both row-wise and column-wise information to improve quantization. They also identify a problem with the zero point when quantizing second moments and address it with a linear quantizer that excludes zero.

Evaluations cover natural language understanding, machine translation, image classification, and instruction tuning. Across all evaluated tasks, the four-bit optimizers achieve accuracy comparable to full-precision counterparts while using memory more efficiently. The findings show that carefully handling the structure of optimizer statistics can enable stronger compression without the accuracy loss that a less suitable quantization scheme might introduce.
neurips-2023-memory-efficient-optimizers.tldr: Carefully designed four-bit quantization compresses optimizer states while preserving comparable accuracy across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting dynamics on a curved surface requires accounting for its geometry. Such surfaces are often represented by meshes, and the partial differential equations defined over them can depend strongly on that geometry. This paper targets a gap between graph networks that overlook surface geometry and geometry-aware architectures that struggle with complex nonlinear dynamics.

The authors introduce a gauge-equivariant architecture based on nonlinear message passing. Gauge equivariance makes the computation consistent with changes in local coordinate conventions on the surface. Combining that geometric property with nonlinear exchanges of information between mesh locations gives the model a way to represent complex dynamics while respecting the structure of the underlying surface.

The architecture achieves better performance than convolutional and attentional alternatives on domains with highly complex nonlinear dynamics. The paper also investigates when message passing provides the greatest benefit. Its conclusion remains task-dependent: design trade-offs can favor convolution, attention, or message passing in different circumstances. The contribution is therefore both a new architecture and an examination of where its particular combination of geometry and nonlinear computation is most useful.
neurips-2023-modeling-dynamics-over-mesh.tldr: Gauge-equivariant nonlinear message passing improves modeling of complex surface dynamics, with benefits that depend on the task.

paragraphs: Predicting activity in mouse primary visual cortex requires understanding the changing visual input experienced during movement. The animal's behavioral state is also thought to strongly affect these responses. This paper studies freely moving mice, addressing a setting that differs substantially from models built around static images shown to head-fixed animals.

The authors develop a multimodal recurrent neural network that combines visual input aligned with the animal's gaze, behavioral information, and temporal dynamics. Recurrence lets the model integrate information over time, matching the continuous nature of natural exploration. An extensive ablation study examines the importance of each component, testing how much the combined prediction depends on these different sources of information.

The model achieves state-of-the-art predictions of V1 activity during free exploration. Analyses using maximally activating stimuli and saliency maps also reveal insights into the modeled responses, including prevalent mixed selectivity for behavioral variables. This suggests that behavioral influences appear in combinations within V1 activity. The framework provides a way to investigate how vision, behavior, and time jointly relate to neural responses during natural movement.
neurips-2023-multimodal-deep-learning-mo.tldr: A recurrent model combining gaze-aligned vision, behavior, and time improves prediction and analysis of V1 activity in freely moving mice.

paragraphs: Learning a model of an unknown dynamical system is useful for control, but some modeling errors matter more to the eventual controller than others. This paper studies how exploration should prioritize those consequential uncertainties in nonlinear systems. Its objective is to learn a controller with low cost on the actual system.

The authors show that minimizing controller loss corresponds to estimating system parameters under a task-dependent metric. This metric expresses which parameter errors are important for the control objective. They then develop an exploration algorithm that reduces uncertainty in that metric, connecting data collection directly to the quality of the controller that will be learned.

A lower-bound analysis establishes that the method learns a controller at a near-instance-optimal rate, relating its efficiency to the difficulty of the particular system. The algorithm uses a general reduction from policy optimization to optimal experiment design in arbitrary systems. Experiments on realistic nonlinear robotic systems demonstrate its effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments support directing exploration toward control-relevant information instead of treating every parameter as equally important.
neurips-2023-optimal-exploration-for-mod.tldr: Task-dependent exploration targets the system parameters most relevant to control and achieves a near-instance-optimal learning rate.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender can influence another decision-maker by choosing what information to reveal. In sequential settings, a farsighted receiver considers future rewards as well as immediate ones. Computing an optimal Markovian signaling scheme in this setting is NP-hard, motivating the paper's reconsideration of the policy class itself.

The authors show that Markovian schemes can be suboptimal and that allowing dependence on interaction history can overcome the stated computational obstacle. The difficulty is representation: a general history-dependent scheme may require more than polynomial space. Their solution is a compact subclass called promise-form schemes, which encode relevant history through honest promises about the receiver's future rewards.

Promise-form schemes are as powerful as general history-dependent schemes while admitting efficient representation. Using them, the authors give an algorithm that computes an optimal, epsilon-persuasive scheme in time polynomial in the instance size and in 1/epsilon. The result combines optimality with an approximate persuasion requirement. It shows how choosing a richer policy class and a suitable compact representation can improve both achievable outcomes and computational tractability.
neurips-2023-persuading-farsighted-recei.tldr: Compact, honest promises enable efficient computation of optimal epsilon-persuasive history-dependent signaling for farsighted receivers.

paragraphs: AI-text detectors can become unreliable when generated text is paraphrased by another language model. RADAR addresses this weakness by making paraphrasing an active part of detector training. The aim is to improve discrimination between human and machine writing even when the machine-generated wording has been deliberately changed to evade detection.

The framework jointly trains a paraphraser and a detector in an adversarial process. The paraphraser tries to produce realistic text that the detector fails to recognize as AI-generated. Feedback from the detector updates the paraphraser, while the paraphraser's outputs help update the detector. This creates an ongoing interaction in which the detector encounters evolving attempts to bypass its decisions.

Experiments using eight language models across four datasets show significant improvements over existing detection methods, particularly when paraphrasing is involved. The authors also report strong transfer from instruction-tuned models to other language models and evaluate improved capability using GPT-3.5-Turbo. These findings support adversarial paraphrasing as a useful training strategy for the tested detection settings, including transfer beyond the models used in a particular training configuration.
neurips-2023-radar-robust-ai-text-detect.tldr: RADAR jointly trains a paraphraser and detector to improve AI-text detection, especially after machine-generated text is paraphrased.

paragraphs: Replicability asks whether an algorithm gives the same output when it receives different samples from the same underlying distribution. The formal requirement studied here is that the outputs be identical with high probability. This is a stronger target than obtaining similar performance across runs, because it concerns agreement in the algorithm's actual result.

The paper brings that requirement into reinforcement learning, where an algorithm learns to make decisions in a control problem. The authors provide a provably replicable algorithm for parallel value iteration and a provably replicable version of R-Max in the episodic setting. These two constructions establish formal replicability results for specific reinforcement-learning procedures.

The contribution extends an emerging line of work on replicable algorithms beyond statistical and batch-learning tasks into control. The abstract emphasizes that control creates different replication challenges from learning on a fixed batch of examples. By supplying proofs for these reinforcement-learning algorithms, the paper establishes that high-probability output agreement can be made an explicit algorithmic guarantee in the studied control settings.
neurips-2023-replicable-reinforcement-le.tldr: The paper establishes formal replicability guarantees for parallel value iteration and episodic R-Max.

paragraphs: Multi-vector search models compare queries and documents through token-level representations, enabling detailed matching. Their scoring can be expensive at large scale. In the process described here, token retrieval first finds candidate documents, after which all token vectors for each candidate are accessed and used to compute its final score.

XTR changes the training objective so that the first retrieval stage preferentially returns the most important document tokens. Better token selection then allows candidates to be ranked using only the retrieved tokens. This connects retrieval and scoring more tightly: the initial stage gathers evidence that is useful enough to support the final ranking without accessing every token representation in each candidate.

The resulting scoring stage is reported to be two to three orders of magnitude cheaper than ColBERT's. On BEIR, XTR improves the state of the art by 2.8 nDCG@10 without distillation. Further analysis finds substantially better token-retrieval recall than ColBERT. The findings show that improving which tokens are retrieved can simultaneously simplify scoring and improve ranking quality in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2023-rethinking-the-role-of-toke.tldr: XTR learns to retrieve important document tokens first, enabling cheaper scoring and stronger retrieval performance.

paragraphs: Training attention-based networks requires retaining intermediate values for the later computation of gradients. Softmax outputs in attention can account for a substantial share of this activation memory. This paper reduces that cost by keeping only a small fraction of those outputs and approximating the discarded values when they are needed.

During the forward pass, the method stores the selected portion of the softmax output and removes the rest from memory. During the backward pass, it reconstructs an approximation of the missing activations and uses it to form gradients. The saving therefore comes from changing what is retained between the two passes, with approximate activation values supporting back-propagation.

Experiments span machine translation, text classification, and sentiment analysis using various attention-based models. The paper reports reductions of up to 84% in the activation memory of the softmax-based attention module, equivalent to 6.2 times less memory, with comparable or better task performance. Reported gains include up to 5.4% higher classification accuracy. These results concern the targeted attention activations and demonstrate their value as a focus for training-memory reduction.
neurips-2023-softmax-output-approximatio.tldr: Keeping only part of attention's softmax output and approximating the rest during back-propagation substantially reduces activation memory.

paragraphs: Combining classifiers can improve prediction, but the size of the benefit varies across settings. This paper investigates when ensembling substantially reduces classification error. Its central comparison is between how often the individual classifiers disagree and how often they are wrong on average, bringing those two quantities into a shared analysis.

The authors prove relationships between the disagreement-error ratio and the relative reduction in error achieved by an ensemble. Large disagreement relative to average error yields significant improvement, while low relative disagreement often means one classifier is sufficient. They also derive improved upper and lower bounds for the test error of a majority-vote classifier under a mild condition they call competence.

Empirical studies across varied settings support the theoretical predictions and identify cases with large and small ensemble gains. A notable distinction appears between interpolating and non-interpolating models: ensembling helps considerably more in the latter group in the reported study. The work therefore offers a more specific basis for assessing ensemble value than simply assuming that adding classifiers will produce a substantial improvement.
neurips-2023-when-are-ensembles-really-e.tldr: Ensembling provides larger gains when classifier disagreement is high relative to their average error rate.
